record_type_quote:
Claim Summary: This replication tests the claim from Kang et al. (2009) that for White

faces, participants would see anger appear sooner and linger longer on an old compared to a

young face, in line with research showing biases against White older adults, which reflects

the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Significant age by race interactions were

observed: while participants perceived anger as lasting longer and appearing sooner on old

compared to young White faces, this relationship was reversed for Black faces, with

participants perceiving anger lasting longer and appearing sooner on young compared to old

Black faces".

targets.authors: Kang, S. K., & Chasteen, A. L.
targets.title: Beyond the double-jeopardy hypothesis: Assessing emotion on the faces of multiply-categorizable targets of prejudice.
targets.evidence_quote:
Claim Summary: This replication tests the claim from Kang et al. (2009) that for White

faces, participants would see anger appear sooner and linger longer on an old compared to a

young face, in line with research showing biases against White older adults, which reflects

the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Significant age by race interactions were

observed: while participants perceived anger as lasting longer and appearing sooner on old

targets.outcome_quote:
For the happy-to-angry transition, analysis revealed a significant two-way interaction

between target age and target race, F(1, 54) = 4.07, p = .049, η²p = 0.07. When observing

Black targets, participants saw anger appear sooner on a young (M = 11.14 s, SD = 3.84 s)

as compared to an old face (M = 12.17, SD = 3.92 s), t(54) = -2.61, p = .012, d = -0.35. The

opposite, however not significant pattern was found for White targets, such that participants

judged anger as appearing sooner on an old (M = 10.68 s, SD = 3.38) as compared to a

young face (M = 13.34 s, SD = 12.70 s), t(54) = 1.47, p = .15. These results are not in line

with the original study and our stated hypotheses, which predicted that for White targets,

participants would judge anger as appearing significantly sooner on an old than on a young

face.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Focal angry-to-happy SCORE test explicitly succeeded, but report also explicitly contrasts other tested original findings: happy-to-angry White effect did not agree, angry-to-neutral Black effect was not fully in line, and neutral-to-angry Black direction was opposite. The success verdict is limited to the key SCORE claim/test, not an overall verdict covering all reported original comparisons. These explicit agreements and contrasts aggregate to mixed.

reasoning: Completed primary SCORE final report by Held and Schütz, matching target, team and claim of assigned SCORE deposit; report dated 2020 while assigned deposit year is 2025. New German sample tests Kang and Chasteen (2009); title and reference identify original unambiguously.
